passage: The pharmacy cooperative in Pema's village had one long counter, and on Monday morning it was full of people waiting for their orders. Varun, the delivery boy, stood at the far door with a crate of syrup bottles, unable to shout over the noise. Pema, at the till, looked up from a receipt and caught his eye. Her eyebrows lifted quickly, a small flick that said, I see you, come in. Varun grinned and nodded, threaded his way through the crowd and put the crate where she pointed. Then she said aloud, "Good morning, Varun-bhai, tea's on the back shelf." The brow flick had been the hello; the words made it certain.

qa.q: What was Varun carrying?
qa.a: He was carrying a crate of syrup bottles.

qa.q: What did Pema mean by her flick of the eyebrows, and how did Varun take it?
qa.a: She meant that she saw him and wanted him to come in, and Varun grinned and nodded, so he understood it as a friendly welcome.

qa.q: Why did Pema follow the flick with a spoken greeting?
qa.a: The flick is easy to overlook, so the words made her hello certain, and she could also offer him tea.

qa.q: How might a customer in the crowd see Pema's quick eyebrow lift?
qa.a: They might not notice it at all, or think it was only a facial habit, since it is a light signal.

grounding: Pema flashes her eyebrows in recognition across a busy counter and follows it with a spoken greeting.

passage: The open-plan office in Warsaw was in the middle of the morning rush, and Olga had headphones on, finishing a report. Across the room, Ines came in with her bag and coat, walked past the coffee machine and caught Olga's eye. Ines's eyebrows lifted briefly and she gave a tiny smile. Olga raised hers back, then pulled off one earphone and called, "Morning! Coffee later?" Ines gave a thumbs-up. Olga remembered the day last week when a new colleague had lifted his brows at her and she had missed it entirely, so he had looked hurt at lunch. Now she made a point of looking up. The eyebrow greeting was a small thing, but it helped the day begin gently.

qa.q: In which city was the office?
qa.a: The office was in Warsaw.

qa.q: What did Ines's raised eyebrows show, and how did Olga feel?
qa.a: They showed recognition and friendliness, and Olga seemed pleased, raising her own brows and calling out an invitation to coffee.

qa.q: What could Olga do to avoid missing such small signals?
qa.a: She could look up now and then and answer with a word or gesture, as she now tries to do.

qa.q: How might the new colleague have felt when Olga missed his eyebrow greeting?
qa.a: He looked hurt at lunch, so he may have felt overlooked, though Olga hadn't meant to ignore him.

grounding: Olga and Ines greet across a room with an eyebrow flash that Olga backs up with words.

passage: In the busy staff canteen of a Mumbai hospital, Kashish, twenty-five, a junior doctor, spotted Sachin, a new pharmacist she'd met once, across the room. Her hands were full with a tray. She caught his eye and flashed her eyebrows up, quick, with a small smile: hello, I remember you. Sachin looked blank and went back to his phone. Kashish felt a little silly. Had he even seen? Maybe he hadn't recognised her. At the drinks counter, she ended up next to him. This time she spoke. "Hi, Sachin! Kashish, from the ward round on Monday." He looked relieved. "Oh, hi! I thought someone was pulling faces at me across the room." She laughed. "That was me. Eyebrow hello." "Ah. Next time wave, I'm terrible at faces." They sat together for lunch, and after that he always raised his eyebrows back.

qa.q: Where had Kashish met Sachin before?
qa.a: On the ward round on Monday.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when Sachin looked blank?
qa.a: She felt a little silly and unsure whether he had seen or recognised her.

qa.q: What made the second greeting work?
qa.a: Kashish added words, her name and where they'd met, so the greeting couldn't be missed.

qa.q: How did Sachin read the eyebrow flash across the room?
qa.a: He thought someone was pulling faces at him, since he's bad at faces and didn't recognise the greeting.

grounding: Shows a young professional's eyebrow flash across a room as a light greeting that is easily missed, so words complement it.

passage:
Dear Ankita,
I've been at the Mumbai office for three weeks, and you told me yesterday that people think I'm a bit cold. I've been thinking about why.
I think it's the eyebrows. In the corridor or across the meeting room, when I see someone I know, I do what I've always done: a quick raise of the eyebrows and a small smile. At home in Goa, everyone does it. It means "hello, I see you, all good." But here I've noticed people say "Hi!" or "Good morning" out loud, or wave. Maybe they don't even notice my eyebrows. Maybe they think I'm ignoring them.
So I'm going to keep my eyebrow hello, because it's me, but add the words too. Starting tomorrow: eyebrows plus "Morning!"
Thank you for telling me honestly. I'd much rather know.
Maria

qa.q: How long has Maria been at the Mumbai office?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling after Ankita said people found Maria cold?
qa.a: Maria felt a bit surprised and thoughtful, and grateful to be told honestly.

qa.q: What does Maria plan to do, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Keep the eyebrow flash but add a spoken "Morning!", since the flash alone is easy to miss.

qa.q: How might colleagues in the Mumbai office have read Maria's eyebrow flash?
qa.a: They may not have noticed it at all, and so thought Maria was ignoring them or being cold.

grounding: Shows a young professional's eyebrow flash as a greeting that others overlook, and adding words to complement it.

passage: Kavitha, you asked for your podcast about small habits at work. Here's mine. I'm Lalremsiami, twenty-six, a nurse on a busy surgical ward in Chennai. There's never time to stop and chat. So when I pass a colleague across the ward, I flash my eyebrows up and smile: quick, silent, friendly. Most of the team knows it now. But a new ward boy, Selvam, joined last month, and for two weeks I flashed my eyebrows at him every morning. He never reacted. I started to wonder if he disliked me. Then one day he said, very politely, "Sister, are you angry with me? You make a face every morning." I laughed so hard. He'd thought my eyebrows were a frown! I told him it was my hello. Now I say, "Good morning, Selvam," out loud as well. He says it back and flashes his own eyebrows, badly. It's our joke now.

qa.q: Where does Lalremsiami work?
qa.a: On a busy surgical ward in Chennai.

qa.q: What was Selvam feeling about the morning eyebrow flash?
qa.a: He was worried and confused, wondering if Lalremsiami was angry with him.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Adding a spoken "Good morning, Selvam" made the greeting clear instead of relying on the easy-to-miss eyebrow flash.

qa.q: What would change if Lalremsiami had never added the spoken greeting?
qa.a: Selvam might have kept thinking she was angry with him every morning, and they would never have shared the joke.

grounding: Shows a young professional using an eyebrow flash as a greeting that others can miss or misread, and complementing it with words.

passage:
I sit near the pantry at the design studio, so I see everyone come in. On Monday Ayesha walked in late, phone at her ear, arms full of fabric samples. Across the room Trisha looked up from her screen. Ayesha couldn't wave or call out, so she lifted both eyebrows quickly, a little flash with half a smile, and kept walking to the meeting room.
Trisha didn't notice; she had already looked back down. I only caught it because I was pouring tea.
At lunch Ayesha stopped by Trisha's desk. "Hey, sorry, I did say hi this morning. Sort of. With my eyebrows."
Trisha laughed. "Honestly? I thought you were ignoring me."
I can't say what either of them was feeling, but they ate together after that, and Ayesha said a proper good morning on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Ayesha carrying when she walked in on Monday?
qa.a: Ayesha had her phone at her ear and her arms full of fabric samples.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha go to Trisha's desk at lunch?
qa.a: Ayesha probably felt a little uneasy that the quick eyebrow flash had been missed and wanted Trisha to know she had been greeted; she may also simply have wanted company for lunch.

qa.q: What could Ayesha try on a busy morning so a greeting isn't missed?
qa.a: She could pair the eyebrow flash with a short hello or a quick message later, since a small facial signal across a room is easy to overlook.

qa.q: How did Trisha read the morning at first?
qa.a: Trisha thought Ayesha was ignoring her, because she never saw the flash and only saw a colleague rush past.

grounding: An eyebrow flash across a room is a light, friendly acknowledgement, but it is easily missed and works best alongside a spoken greeting.
